entry.title: Inside the Wan2.2 VAE Decoder
entry.content:
Introduction

A variational autoencoder (VAE) consists of an encoder and a decoder. The encoder compresses images or videos into latents, while the decoder reconstructs the original input from these latents. Because this compression is lossy, the reconstructed pixels approximate the original input, as illustrated in Figure 1.

Figure 1: Encoding into latents and decoding back to pixels.

Scroll figures sideways to see the full diagram.

VAEs in Video Generation

In text-to-video generation, the diffusion model operates in latent space, reducing the computation required compared to generating pixels directly. Starting from noise, it repeatedly denoises the latents conditioned on the text prompt. The VAE decoder then converts the resulting latents into RGB frames. As shown in Figure 2, the decoder receives its input from the diffusion model rather than the VAE encoder.

Figure 2: The VAE decoder turns generated latents into video.

Cosmos3-Nano uses the Wan2.2 VAE from Wan2.2-TI2V-5B.

Decoder Architecture

Figure 3 shows the decoder stages for a 720p video with 189 frames.

Figure 3: Main decoder stages and output shapes for the 720p example.

Input Projection

The decoder first reverses the latent normalization and applies a 1 × 1 × 1 Conv3D projection. At each position, this projection computes a learned linear combination of the 48 input channels to produce 48 output channels. Because the kernel spans only one position, it mixes channels without reading neighboring positions or changing the tensor shape.

A 3 × 3 × 3 causal Conv3D then expands the channel dimension from 48 to 1,024, preserving the 48 × 45 × 80 grid. With kernel dimensions ordered as time × height × width, each output combines a 3 × 3 spatial neighborhood from the current and two preceding time steps. Restricting the temporal window to current and past inputs makes the convolution causal. Missing earlier inputs are padded with zeros. Figure 4 illustrates these dependencies.

Figure 4: Three spatial neighborhoods contribute to one output. Future time steps are excluded.

Residual Blocks and Spatial Attention

Before upsampling, the decoder applies two residual blocks with spatial attention between them, as shown in Figure 5. These operations preserve the 48 × 45 × 80 × 1024 shape while combining information from neighboring positions through convolutions and across the spatial grid through attention.

Each residual block applies two sequences of RMS normalization, SiLU, and causal Conv3D, then adds the skip connection.

Figure 5: Residual blocks and spatial attention, each with an input skip connection. Normalization and activation within the residual paths are omitted.

Spatial attention operates independently at each time step. After normalization, a 1 × 1 Conv2D projects the 1,024 input channels into queries, keys, and values, each with 1,024 channels. The 45 × 80 spatial grid is then flattened into 3,600 positions for attention. The attention output is reshaped back to the grid and projected through a final 1 × 1 Conv2D, before adding the block’s input through the skip connection.

Temporal and Spatial Upsampling

Temporal upsampling increases the number of time steps, while spatial upsampling increases height and width at each time step. Both operate on intermediate features, which are not yet RGB frames.

Three stages expand the feature grid from 48 × 45 × 80 × 1024 to 189 × 360 × 640 × 512. The first two expand time and space, while the third expands only space. Each stage contains residual blocks, upsampling, and a skip connection, as shown in Figure 6.

Figure 6: Each stage refines features, upsamples, then adds a matching stage skip connection. The residual blocks also have their own internal skip connections, omitted here.

Each stage begins with three residual blocks that preserve the temporal and spatial dimensions. In the third stage, the first block also reduces the channel dimension from 1,024 to 512, requiring a learned projection on its skip connection. The remaining blocks preserve the channel dimension and therefore use identity skip connections.

Temporal upsampling uses a 3 × 1 × 1 causal Conv3D to predict twice as many channels at each spatial position, providing the values for both output steps. Reshaping separates these values into two time steps, each with the original channel count. For example, with two channels per step:

Figure 7: Four predicted channel values rearranged into two time steps.

The two output steps can have different values because the convolution predicts them separately. Since the first input step is not expanded, a stage with T input steps produces 1 + 2(T − 1) output steps. The two temporal upsampling stages therefore increase the sequence length from 48 → 95 → 189 steps.

Spatial upsampling enlarges the feature grid at each time step without changing the number of time steps. Nearest-neighbor resizing copies each feature vector into a 2 × 2 area, doubling height and width—for example, from 45 × 80 → 90 × 160. A 3 × 3 Conv2D then mixes neighboring features within each time step. All three stages perform spatial upsampling, increasing the grid from 45 × 80 → 90 × 160 → 180 × 320 → 360 × 640. In the first two stages, this follows temporal upsampling.

The Repeat-and-Reshape Skip Connection

In addition to the skip connections within individual residual blocks, each stage has a stage skip connection, shown in purple in Figure 6. This branch bypasses both the residual blocks and the upsampling operations. To make its output compatible with the main branch, it repeats and rearranges channel values without learned weights. The two branches are then added elementwise.

Stages 1 and 2: expand time and space.

At one input position, each channel value a is repeated across four spatial positions at each of two consecutive output time steps. This produces two 2 × 2 patches with the same channel count:

Figure 8: One channel value repeated across spatial positions and time steps.

This operation is applied independently to each of the 1,024 channels, matching the spatial and temporal expansion of the main branch.

Stage 3: expand space and halve the channels.

At each spatial position, the skip connection takes a pair of input channels and maps their values into one output channel’s 2 × 2 patch. If the two values are a and b, repeating each value twice fills the patch as follows:

Figure 9: Two channels at one input position mapped into one channel over four output positions.

Each pair of input channels therefore becomes one output channel spread across four spatial positions. This halves the channel count from 1,024 to 512 while doubling height and width. The number of time steps stays unchanged.

Both input values are preserved in the patch, with no averaging or learned weights. The main branch reaches the same output shape through its convolutions and spatial upsampling, allowing the two branches to be added.

Output Reconstruction

At this point, each position in the 189 × 360 × 640 grid contains 512 feature values. Output reconstruction converts these features into RGB pixels. It first reduces the channel count, then predicts the values for four pixels at each position, and finally arranges those pixels into the full-resolution frames.

Figure 10: Output reconstruction, from decoder features to RGB frames.

The output head applies RMS normalization, SiLU, and a 3 × 3 × 3 causal Conv3D to predict 12 values at each grid position: the RGB values for four pixels. Unpacking then rearranges the 12 predicted values at each position into a 2 × 2 patch of RGB pixels, doubling height and width without changing the number of frames.

Final Residual Blocks

The final three residual blocks reduce the channel count from 512 to 256, keeping the number of time steps, height, and width unchanged. The first block performs this reduction in its first convolution and uses a 1 × 1 × 1 Conv3D on the skip connection to match. The remaining convolutions preserve 256 channels, and the next two blocks use identity skip connections.

Figure 11: The three final residual blocks. Only the first block changes the channel count.

References

  • Wan2.2 VAE implementation: decoder architecture, convolutions, attention, upsampling, and repeat-and-reshape skip connections.
  • Cosmos3-Nano VAE configuration: the Wan2.2 model configuration used for this article.

link.title: Dynamic Parameter Offloading for LLM Serving

entry.content:
Introduction

Part 1 introduced the memory constraints in LLM serving. Part 2 examined vLLM on the GH200 and motivated three requirements for parameter offloading: asynchronous prefetching, compatibility with CUDA graphs, and adaptation to changing workloads.

In this final post, we describe our dynamic parameter offloading system, implemented in vLLM , and evaluate its performance and limitations.

Design

This section presents the design of a serving system that dynamically offloads model parameters from GPU HBM to CPU memory on the GH200, repurposing the freed memory for KV cache to support larger batch sizes. Offloaded parameters are stored in contiguous CPU tensors and asynchronously prefetched to the GPU ahead of execution, exploiting the GH200’s high CPU to GPU bandwidth to overlap data movement with computation. Unlike static offloading strategies, the system continuously adjusts the degree of offloading at runtime based on current KV cache pressure and estimated iteration latency, aiming to maximize overall throughput. We first motivate the core tradeoff between offloading overhead and KV cache capacity, then describe the mechanisms for asynchronous parameter transfer, dynamic memory management, and the policy that drives offloading decisions.

Overview

The system is implemented within vLLM’s V1 engine and introduces three components: an OffloadManager that decides how many layers to offload based on KV cache pressure and estimated iteration latency, a dynamic KV cache queue that adjusts available KV cache capacity at runtime as the offloading configuration changes, and a context manager that handles asynchronous prefetching and GPU memory management for offloaded parameters. At each scheduling step, the OffloadManager evaluates whether to adjust the current offloading level, and the scheduler executes the new configuration in the following iteration.

The KV Cache and Offloading Tradeoff

When GPU memory already suffices for the KV cache, offloading model parameters to CPU is pure overhead. Under higher load, offloading frees GPU memory for additional concurrent requests. However, the throughput gain is not monotonic in the number of offloaded layers: each layer freed provides a fixed amount of KV cache capacity, but transfer overhead grows with each additional layer, and beyond a certain batch size the GPU becomes compute-bound regardless. The optimal offloading depth therefore depends on the current workload, which shifts as request rates and sequence lengths change at runtime.

Existing offloading systems adjust this balance dynamically but use transfer-hiding as the stopping criterion. Oneiros offloads model layers to CPU and monitors GPU computation time, capping the number of offloaded layers so that parameter transfers complete within each iteration. Pie offloads KV cache rather than parameters, incrementally moving KV cache blocks to CPU memory until swap latency is about to exceed computation latency. Despite targeting different data, both systems constrain offloading to hide transfer time behind computation. This is overly conservative: even when transfers exceed computation time, the additional KV cache capacity can enable sufficiently larger batches that improve the overall throughput.

To determine how many layers to offload, we monitor estimated decode throughput. We use KV cache capacity divided by iteration time as a proxy for tokens per second. KV cache capacity bounds the number of concurrent requests, and each request generates one token per decode iteration, so this ratio approximates the system’s effective throughput. We continue increasing offloading as long as the larger batch size enabled by the additional memory outweighs the overhead of longer iteration times.

Asynchronous Parameter Offloading

We offload model parameters rather than KV cache for two reasons rooted in the GH200’s memory-system characteristics (Memory System Performance in Part 2).

First, parameters are read-only during inference. Once a layer’s weights have been copied to CPU memory, they never need to be written back, so every subsequent transfer is a CPU to GPU read. This eliminates bidirectional traffic and sidesteps the directional asymmetry of the C2C link, where GPU to CPU bandwidth is notably lower.

Second, the weights of a single transformer layer can be packed into a single contiguous tensor on the CPU side. A single cudaMemcpyAsync per layer maximizes the effective transfer size and keeps the copy close to the link’s peak throughput, avoiding the overhead of many small, scattered transfers.

Layer Placement Strategy

Transformer models execute their layers sequentially, from layer $0$ to layer $N-1$. This highly predictable execution path allows the system to know exactly when a specific layer will be needed. To exploit this predictability, we divide the $N$ total model layers into two distinct groups based on a configurable parameter $k$: we keep $N - 2k$ layers in dedicated GPU memory, and we offload the remaining $2k$ layers to pinned CPU memory.

For the $2k$ offloaded layers, the system allocates $k$ shared GPU memory regions. The offloaded layers are organized into $k$ distinct pairs, with each pair sharing a single GPU memory region. For the even-layer models considered here, we maximize the available prefetch window by pairing layers separated by $N/2$ positions in the execution order. This means that layer $i$ is paired with layer $i + N/2$ for $i=0, \ldots, k-1$. Figure 1 illustrates this configuration for a model with $N=8$ layers and an offloading depth of $k=2$.

Figure 1: Layer placement with $N=8$ layers and an offloading depth of $k=2$.

During the forward pass, when the first layer in a pair completes its computation, the system immediately issues an asynchronous copy to fetch the parameters of the second layer from the CPU into their shared GPU memory region. Because execution is strictly sequential, $N/2-1$ layers run before the second layer is needed, giving the transfer the largest possible time window to complete behind ongoing GPU compute. Figure 2 demonstrates an execution timeline that hides the transfer latency with $N=8$ layers and an offloading depth of $k=2$.

Figure 2: Prefetch scheduling with $N=8$ layers and an offloading depth of $k=2$.

This strategy frees GPU memory equivalent to $k$ layers. The system can scale this offloading depth up to a maximum of $k = \lfloor N/2 \rfloor$. For an even number of equally sized layers, this pairs all layers and reclaims half of their parameter memory for the KV cache.

Transfer Mechanism

Offloaded layers are transferred from their pinned CPU tensors into the shared GPU memory regions on dedicated CUDA streams. These streams operate independently from the main compute stream. Each transfer is issued concurrently with the execution of the preceding layer. The system synchronizes these parallel streams using CUDA events. This strict synchronization guarantees that the parameters for an offloaded layer are fully resident on the GPU before its forward pass begins.

The synchronization points between the transfer and compute streams are implemented as custom operations within the piecewise CUDA graph execution of vLLM. This architecture natively supports inserting uncaptured operations between graph segments. By handling synchronization between the segments rather than inside them, the system completely avoids the severe latency penalty of triggering new graph captures whenever the dynamic offloading level changes.

Dynamic Memory Management

Changing the offloading level at runtime requires reallocating GPU memory between model parameters and KV cache. However, CUDA graphs capture fixed virtual memory addresses at record time. Any reallocation that changes the virtual addresses of weight or KV cache tensors would invalidate all recorded graphs, forcing expensive re-captures, which is infeasible while serving requests at runtime.

Custom Virtual Memory Allocator

To decouple virtual addresses from physical memory backing, we build on KVCached , a VMM-based allocator originally designed for managing KV cache tensors. KVCached already provides fragmentation-aware page allocation and a zero page mechanism for CUDA graph compatibility. We generalize its design to support tensors of arbitrary shapes, which is necessary for managing both KV cache blocks and shared GPU memory regions, and extend it with additional operations that allow physical pages to be shared across virtual address ranges.

The allocator reserves large contiguous virtual address ranges at initialization but lazily commits physical pages on demand via CUDA’s Virtual Memory Management API. Because virtual addresses are fixed at reservation time and never change, CUDA graphs remain valid even as the physical memory behind those addresses is remapped. To ensure that all virtual addresses remain valid at all times, unmapped regions are backed by a single shared zero page rather than left unaddressed. This guarantees that any GPU access to an unmapped region produces a deterministic zero read instead of a segmentation fault, allowing CUDA graphs to safely reference the full virtual address range regardless of the current physical mapping state.

The allocator exposes page-granularity operations through a C++/pybind11 extension: map and unmap commit or release physical pages at specified offsets within a named tensor, replacing released mappings with the zero page. map_pages_to_tensor maps physical pages from one virtual tensor onto another, allowing both tensors to reference the same physical memory. For example, this enables the system to remap model parameter pages onto the shared memory regions or resize the KV cache tensor without any data copies or changes to virtual addresses.

Group-Aligned KV Cache Resizing

Changing the offloading level requires adjusting the number of KV cache blocks available to the scheduler. When layers are offloaded, the freed GPU memory is mapped into the KV cache tensor and the corresponding block IDs are added to the block manager’s free list. When layers are reclaimed, the reverse must occur: blocks are removed from the free list and their physical pages are remapped to shared memory regions.

In our implementation, physical memory is mapped at a granularity of 2 MB. Individual KV cache blocks are typically 64 to 256 KB, so a single 2 MB page spans multiple blocks. Freeing an arbitrary block risks deallocating memory that backs a neighboring block still in use. We address this by organizing blocks into groups of contiguous blocks that together align to 2 MB page boundaries.

We adopt vLLM’s interleaved KV cache layout , which stores all layers’ KV data in a single contiguous tensor. Because each block now holds KV data for all layers, the effective block size is the product of the number of layers and the per-layer block size. For example, a 32-layer model with 128 KB per layer per block yields 4 MB blocks, which are natively 2 MB-aligned. When the block size is not a multiple of 2 MB, such as 1.5 MB blocks, we group a small number of contiguous blocks until the total reaches a 2 MB boundary (four blocks in this case). Since model dimensions are typically powers of two, most configurations require only one or two blocks per group. Figure 3 illustrates a case with 4 blocks per group where Group 1 cannot be deallocated despite 3 of its 4 blocks being free.

Figure 3: Group-aligned KV cache resizing with 4 blocks per group.

Reclamation operates at group granularity, meaning only groups whose blocks are all free can be unmapped. When the scheduler requests reclamation of a tier (the blocks corresponding to one offloading level), two cases arise. If enough complete groups are already free, they are removed immediately. Otherwise, the system enters a draining state where freed blocks accumulate in a separate reclaim queue as requests complete and release their KV cache. Once sufficient complete groups have accumulated, the reclaim completes and remaining blocks are returned to the main free list. If KV cache pressure rises during draining, for example because the main free list is exhausted, the drain is aborted and all reclaim-queue blocks are spliced back into the main queue, preserving availability. This ensures that resizing never blocks the scheduler and adapts gracefully to shifting demand.

Offloading Policy

As discussed in The KV Cache and Offloading Tradeoff, increasing the offloading depth does not monotonically improve throughput. We observe that even with full compute–transfer overlap, decode latency grows linearly with the number of offloaded layers, while compute-dominated prefill and mixed iterations show a less dramatic slowdown. Because decode iterations are most sensitive to offloading overhead and constitute the majority of iterations under sustained load, the policy uses a decode-throughput proxy: the number of available KV cache blocks divided by average decode iteration time.

Modeling Decode Latency

The system must estimate decode latency at each offloading level without relying on extensive offline profiling. We measure forward-pass time every iteration and maintain an average of decode latency per offloading level, filtering out iterations that contain prefill requests (which are identifiable from the scheduler metadata). To bootstrap these estimates, the system starts at the maximum offloading depth and steps down one level at a time during warmup, recording a conservative lower bound on decode latency at each level before settling into steady-state operation.

Decision Rule

At each scheduling step, the policy evaluates whether to adjust the current offloading level $k$ based on two signals: KV cache pressure and estimated decode throughput. Algorithm 1 illustrates the policy.

The policy distinguishes two pressure regimes. High pressure occurs when requests are waiting in the queue or KV cache utilization exceeds a threshold $\tau_h$. Low pressure occurs when no requests are waiting and utilization falls below a lower threshold $\tau_l$. If neither condition holds, the current level is retained.

Under high pressure. The policy considers increasing offloading by one level. It calculates the throughput proxy $E[T_k]$ for a given level $k$ as:

\[E[T_k] = \frac{C_k}{L_k}\]

where $C_k$ is the KV cache capacity in blocks and $L_k$ is the average decode latency at that level. This score has units of blocks per unit time; it is a proxy for comparing offloading levels, not a direct measurement of tokens per second. The system compares the estimates for the current level $k$ and the next level $k+1$. The transition to $k+1$ is enacted only if $E[T_{k+1}] > E[T_k]$.

Under low pressure. The policy decreases offloading by one level unconditionally. Since the freed KV cache capacity is currently unutilized, reducing the offloading level safely reduces iteration latency without impacting concurrent request capacity.

Algorithm 1: Dynamic offloading policy evaluation (per iteration).

Inputs: current offloading level $k$, cooldown timer $c$, cooldown period $C$, queue length $Q$, KV cache utilization $U$, utilization thresholds $\tau_h$ and $\tau_l$, and maximum offloading level $M = \lfloor N/2 \rfloor$. The capacity and latency arrays contain $C_k$ and $L_k$ for each level.

# Pseudocode; update both the offloading level and the cooldown state.
if cooldown_remaining > 0:
    cooldown_remaining -= 1
    return level, cooldown_remaining

if queue_length > 0 or kv_utilization > high_threshold:
    if level < max_level:
        current_throughput = capacity[level] / decode_latency[level]
        next_throughput = capacity[level + 1] / decode_latency[level + 1]
        if next_throughput > current_throughput:
            level += 1
            cooldown_remaining = cooldown_period
elif queue_length == 0 and kv_utilization < low_threshold:
    if level > 0:
        level -= 1
        cooldown_remaining = cooldown_period

return level, cooldown_remaining

After any level change, a cooldown of $C$ iterations suppresses further decisions. This window allows the latency estimates $L_k$ to stabilize at the new configuration before the policy evaluates further transitions.

Limitations

By design, every byte of GPU memory reclaimed for the KV cache requires two bytes of pinned CPU memory. While this tradeoff enables significantly faster unidirectional transfers, it can become a bottleneck when serving very large models under tight CPU memory constraints. In such cases, a bidirectional approach could help reduce the CPU memory footprint: rather than maintaining copies in both GPU and CPU memory simultaneously, each layer would reside exclusively in one location at any given time, with background transfers migrating layers between devices as needed. Additionally, allowing more than two layers to share a single GPU memory region could further reduce the pinned CPU memory required.

The current implementation relies on vLLM’s piecewise CUDA graph execution to insert synchronization and transfer operations between graph segments. While full CUDA graphs would further reduce kernel launch overhead, the performance difference is minimal in practice, as shown in Execution Optimizations in Part 2. Furthermore, future work could involve full CUDA graphs for the attention computation while only introducing graph splits strictly for the synchronization and transfer operations.

Additionally, while the policy can operate without prior measurements by starting at maximum offloading and adjusting reactively, our experiments use an initial warmup phase that steps through each offloading level to collect decode latency estimates before entering steady state operation. This requires processing a single request at each level, so warmup time scales linearly with the number of offloading levels and depends on how quickly requests arrive. Under moderate load, this adds negligible overhead relative to total serving time, but it delays the system from reaching its optimal configuration until the warmup phase completes.

Implementation Summary

The system is implemented on top of vLLM v0.13.0, comprising roughly 7,000 LoC: 5,800 lines of Python for vLLM integration and 1,200 lines of C++ for the custom virtual memory allocator package extending KVCached’s VMM API management. The implementation touches three core modules: the V1 scheduler (offloading policy and KV cache resizing), the model executor (prefetch pipeline and graph integration), and worker initialization (memory allocator setup). All changes maintain compatibility with vLLM’s existing features including tensor/pipeline parallelism, prefix caching, and chunked prefill.

Evaluation

Baselines

As shown in Execution Optimizations in Part 2, vLLM’s existing offloading mechanisms provide limited benefit for throughput: UVA parameter offloading degrades decode latency due to synchronous parameter fetching, while KV cache offloading does not free GPU memory for additional concurrent requests, serving primarily as an extended prefix cache tier. We therefore evaluate our system against default vLLM v0.13.0 as the primary baseline.

We do not compare directly against Pie, Oneiros, or SuperInfer for several reasons. All three systems are built on vLLM’s V0 engine, which lacks several optimizations enabled by default in V1, including full CUDA graph support, the optimized contiguous KV cache layout, and improved scheduling — making cross-engine comparisons reflect engine differences rather than offloading strategy differences. Additionally, SuperInfer’s implementation is not publicly available. Furthermore, none of the three systems support prefix caching, which is enabled by default in our system and in production vLLM deployments. Disabling prefix caching to match their configuration would penalize our system on workloads with prefix overlap, while enabling it would give us an advantage unrelated to offloading. Instead, we evaluate against vLLM’s own offloading mechanisms on the same engine version, pinpointing the exact contribution of our design choices.

Experimental Setup

Hardware, models, workloads, and metrics are as described in Experimental Setup in Part 2. As in that section, we use an open-loop Poisson workload and report achieved throughput (completed requests divided by the time window length) as the request rate. Request rate ranges are chosen per model to span from low load to beyond saturation, with specific ranges reported in each subsection. Each configuration is run a minimum of five times at each request rate.

Our experiments were conducted on shared cluster nodes, where we occasionally observe runs with virtual memory remapping latency degraded by 2–10 $\times$ compared to the expected baseline, indicating system-level interference unrelated to our system. We identify such runs using a remapping latency threshold determined independently of end-to-end performance metrics: 180 ms for Qwen3-32B and Llama 3.1-70B FP8, and 1000 ms for Mixtral-8x22B. Across all experiments, 6% of Qwen3-32B runs, 9% of Llama 3.1-70B FP8, and 17% of Mixtral-8x22B runs were excluded under this criterion. Beyond remapping latency outliers, we also observed that available GPU memory can vary by 1–2 GB between runs on the same node, depending on cluster-wide usage. This variability contributes to performance differences across repetitions, as reflected by the error bars in our plots.

We limit the maximum offloading depth for Mixtral-8x22B to 40 layers due to out-of-memory errors during dynamic resizing at higher levels. In practice, this constraint does not affect our results: the decode latency overhead at 40 sharded layers is already sufficiently high that the dynamic policy consistently converges to lower offloading levels to maximize throughput.

Microbenchmarks

Before evaluating end-to-end serving performance, we validate the core mechanisms of our system in isolation. We measure achieved parameter transfer throughput to verify that our contiguous tensor layout saturates the NVLink-C2C interconnect, and quantify the per-iteration overhead introduced by offloading across decode, prefill, and mixed iterations. These measurements confirm that the building blocks perform as expected and provide context for interpreting the end-to-end results that follow.

Achieved Transfer Throughput

Figure 4 reports the achieved CPU to GPU transfer throughput for each model. All values are reported per GPU; for Mixtral-8x22B, each layer is sharded across 4 GPUs via tensor parallelism, so the per-GPU transfer throughput reflects the sharded partition.

For a low number of offloaded layers, Qwen3-32B and Llama 3.1-70B achieve a lower transfer throughput compared to higher offloading depths. We suspect that in these cases the CPU to GPU transfer is not the bottleneck, but the HBM accesses during decode iterations which interfere with the transfer. The effect of this interference is less noticeable as we offload more layers since it is amortized by the increased CPU to GPU traffic. This pattern is not visible for Mixtral-8x22B, which we suspect is bound by tensor parallelism communication (e.g., NCCL AllReduce) at low-offload levels rather than HBM memory bandwidth.

Figure 4: Achieved transfer throughput versus the number of offloaded layers for Qwen3-32B, Llama 3.1-70B FP8, and Mixtral-8x22B.

All three configurations achieve approximately 392 GB/s at high offloading levels, corresponding to roughly 87% of the peak theoretical unidirectional NVLink-C2C bandwidth of 450 GB/s. Throughput is consistent across models despite varying layer sizes, confirming that all transfers exceed the saturation threshold identified in Memory System Performance in Part 2.

Per-Iteration Offloading Overhead

Figure 5 reports the per-iteration cost of offloading as a function of the number of offloaded layers. We measure forward pass time and split measurements based on whether the iteration contains prefill requests, as prefill iterations are compute-dominated and provide more opportunity to overlap transfers with computation. The red line shows the KV cache capacity gained at each offloading level.

Figure 5: Iteration time and available KV cache capacity at varying number of offloaded layers at 10.0, 7.0, and 20.0 RPS target arrival rate for Qwen3-32B, Llama 3.1-70B FP8, and Mixtral-8x22B, respectively.

Across all three models, decode iteration time grows approximately linearly with the number of offloaded layers, while prefill iterations show a much smaller relative increase, confirming that offloading overhead is largely hidden behind prefill computation. For Qwen3-32B, decode time grows from approximately 25 ms to 135 ms at maximum offloading, while KV cache capacity nearly triples from approximately 14 GB to 40 GB. Part of this increase is due to larger batch sizes, as the additional KV cache capacity allows the scheduler to admit more concurrent requests.

The two other models illustrate why offloading overhead varies across configurations. FP8 quantization halves the parameter size per layer, directly reducing the transfer volume per offloaded layer by 2x. However, the compute speedup is smaller because only matrix multiplications benefit from FP8 tensor cores, while operations such as softmax and layer normalization remain in higher precision. This asymmetry means transfer overhead shrinks faster than the compute window available to hide it, which is why Llama 3.1-70B FP8 shows lower offloading decode overhead than Qwen3-32B despite having more layers. Similarly, tensor parallelism adds inter-GPU communication overhead to every iteration, extending the compute window, while each GPU only transfers its sharded partition rather than the full layer. Consequently, Mixtral-8x22B also shows a lower offloading overhead increment.

These results illustrate the core tradeoff that the dynamic policy must navigate: each additional offloading level provides a fixed increment of KV cache capacity at the cost of increasing decode latency. Both quantization and tensor parallelism shift this tradeoff favorably, allowing more layers to be offloaded before the overhead outweighs the capacity gain.

Dynamic Resizing Cost

Table 1 reports the cost of a single offloading level transition, which is dominated by remapping virtual memory pages for both KV cache and model parameter tensors. Qwen3-32B and Llama 3.1-70B FP8 complete a transition in approximately 130 ms, consistent with their similar page counts. Mixtral-8x22B requires roughly 7x longer despite having only 5x more pages. Virtual memory remapping operations are issued sequentially across all four GPUs, and the super-linear scaling suggests there may be additional contention on shared driver or interconnect resources. These results highlight the importance of the cooldown mechanism in Algorithm 1 in the dynamic policy: by ensuring the system operates at a stable offloading level for many iterations between transitions, the resizing cost is amortized over a large number of iterations. Reducing this overhead for multi-GPU configurations remains an open challenge.

Model GPUs Total pages to remap Resizing cost (ms)
Qwen3-32B 1 1888 130.29 ± 12.49
Llama 3.1-70B 1 1700 130.15 ± 24.35
Mixtral-8x22B 4 9696 939.99 ± 26.23
Table 1: Dynamic KV cache resizing cost per offloading level transition.

End-to-End Serving Performance

We evaluate end-to-end serving performance across three model configurations, each highlighting a different aspect of the system. Qwen3-32B serves as the baseline single-GPU evaluation, Llama 3.1-70B FP8 demonstrates the interaction between quantization and offloading, and Mixtral-8x22B validates the system under 4-way tensor parallelism. For each model, we sweep request rates from low load to beyond saturation and report median and P99 time to first token (TTFT), end-to-end latency (E2E), and time between tokens (TBT) over 1,800-second runs. We define the saturation point as the maximum request rate achieved by the respective system. As noted in Experimental Setup, shared cluster interference and GPU memory variability between runs contribute to wider error bars at some request rates.

Single-GPU (Qwen3-32B)

Figure 6 reports median TTFT, E2E latency, and TBT for Qwen3-32B on ShareGPT across increasing request rates. Default vLLM saturates at approximately 13.5 requests per second, beyond which TTFT and E2E latency rise sharply as requests accumulate in the queue. Our system sustains up to 14.8 requests per second before saturating, a 10% improvement in maximum sustainable throughput. The additional KV cache capacity from dynamic offloading allows the scheduler to admit more concurrent requests, reducing queueing delays. TBT increases moderately at higher request rates due to the offloading overhead during decode iterations, consistent with the per-iteration measurements in Microbenchmarks. This tradeoff is favorable: the reduction in TTFT and E2E latency significantly outweighs the modest increase in TBT.

Figure 6: Evaluation of Qwen3-32B at varying request rates on ShareGPT.

At moderate to high request rates (13.0 to 15.0), our system achieves lower P99 TBT than default vLLM despite offloading overhead. At this load, default vLLM begins experiencing preemptions, where evicted requests must recompute their KV cache when rescheduled, causing latency spikes that disproportionately affect tail latency. The additional KV cache capacity from offloading avoids these preemptions, resulting in lower P99 TBT. At higher request rates, the larger batch sizes enabled by offloading increase per-iteration compute, and P99 TBT rises above the baseline.

Figure 7 shows the CDF at a target arrival rate of 14.5, which is above the saturation point of default vLLM. While default vLLM queues most requests for tens of seconds before processing, our system serves the majority of requests almost immediately. E2E latency shows a similar improvement. TBT increases slightly due to offloading overhead, but this is a favorable tradeoff compared to the order-of-magnitude reduction in queueing delay.

Figure 7: CDF of Qwen3-32B on ShareGPT at a target arrival rate of 14.5 RPS.

Single-GPU Quantized (Llama 3.1-70B FP8)

Figure 8 reports median and P99 latency metrics for Llama 3.1-70B FP8 across request rates. Default vLLM saturates at approximately 8.7 requests per second, while our system sustains up to 10.1 requests per second. As predicted by the microbenchmarks, the reduced per-layer transfer volume from FP8 quantization allows more layers to be offloaded before the overhead outweighs the capacity gain, resulting in a 16% improvement in maximum sustainable throughput compared to 10% for Qwen3-32B.

Figure 8: Evaluation of Llama 3.1-70B FP8 at varying request rates on ShareGPT.

Figure 9 shows the CDF at a target arrival rate of 10.0 RPS, which is above the saturation point of default vLLM. Similarly to Qwen3-32B, our system eliminates most queueing delay while incurring only a modest increase in TBT.

Figure 9: CDF of Llama 3.1-70B FP8 on ShareGPT at a target arrival rate of 10.0 RPS.

Multi-GPU (Mixtral-8x22B, 4-GPU TP)

Figure 10 reports median and P99 latency metrics for Mixtral-8x22B across request rates. Default vLLM saturates at approximately 20.5 requests per second, while our system sustains up to 25.1 requests per second, a 22% improvement in maximum sustainable throughput. As predicted by the microbenchmarks, tensor parallelism extends the per-iteration compute window through inter-GPU communication while reducing the transfer volume per GPU, allowing more layers to be offloaded before the overhead outweighs the capacity gain. This results in a larger throughput improvement compared to the 10% observed for Qwen3-32B.

Figure 10: Evaluation of Mixtral-8x22B at varying request rates on ShareGPT.

Figure 11 shows the CDF at a target arrival rate of 25.0 RPS, which is above the saturation point of default vLLM. Our system again eliminates most queueing delay, substantially reducing TTFT and E2E latency. The increase in TBT is more pronounced than for the single-GPU models, which we analyze in detail in Dynamic Policy Behavior.

Figure 11: CDF of Mixtral-8x22B on ShareGPT at a target arrival rate of 25.0 RPS.

Dynamic Policy Behavior

The previous sections evaluated aggregate performance across entire runs. Here we examine how the dynamic policy adapts in real time by inspecting time-series traces of offloading level, KV cache utilization, and request queue depth. We present two cases: Llama 3.1-70B, where the policy operates smoothly, and Mixtral-8x22B, where multi-GPU limitations expose current shortcomings. At low request rates, the dynamic policy reduces offloading to a minimal level and our system performs comparably to default vLLM; detailed low request rate results are provided in Appendix A: Low RPS Evaluation.

Single-GPU with Aligned KV Cache Blocks

Both Qwen3-32B and Llama 3.1-70B FP8 have 2 MB-aligned KV cache block sizes, allowing the policy to reclaim individual blocks without grouping constraints. Their dynamic behavior is similar. We include the Qwen3-32B trace in Appendix B: High RPS Evaluation and present Llama 3.1-70B FP8 here as a representative example.

Figure 12: Trace of Llama 3.1-70B FP8 on ShareGPT at a target arrival rate of 10.0 RPS.

Figure 12 shows a trace at a target arrival rate of 10.0 RPS. Default vLLM’s waiting queue grows continuously, accumulating over 2000 pending requests, confirming this rate exceeds its capacity. Our system keeps the queue near zero throughout. The policy adjusts offloading between 0 and 24 offloaded layers in response to KV cache pressure, increasing offloading when utilization rises and decreasing offloading when it decreases. Despite serving more concurrent requests, the waiting queue remains empty, demonstrating that the throughput gained from larger batch sizes outweighs the offloading overhead.

Multi-GPU with Misaligned KV Cache Blocks

Mixtral-8x22B has a per-block KV cache size of 1.75 MB, which does not align to the 2 MB page granularity required by the CUDA VMM API. The system therefore groups 8 contiguous blocks into a single reclaimable unit, meaning all 8 blocks must be free before their backing memory can be remapped. This coarser reclamation granularity makes the policy less reactive: when the policy decides to reduce offloading, it must wait for an entire group to drain before memory can be reclaimed, delaying the transition. Combined with the higher resizing cost observed in the microbenchmarks, this explains the more pronounced TBT increase for Mixtral-8x22B noted in End-to-End Serving Performance.

Figure 13: Trace of Mixtral-8x22B on ShareGPT at a target arrival rate of 25.0 RPS.

Figure 13 shows a trace of Mixtral-8x22B at a target arrival rate of 25.0 RPS. As with the single-GPU case, default vLLM’s queue grows unboundedly while our system keeps it near zero. However, the number of offloaded layers panel reveals a staircase pattern compared to the peaks seen for Llama 3.1-70B FP8. Increasing offloading remains fast, as freed parameter memory can be immediately mapped into the KV cache. Decreasing offloading is more difficult: reducing an offloading level requires waiting for an entire group of 8 blocks to become free, which depends on when in-flight requests complete and release their KV cache. This is visible around 900 seconds, where the policy cannot decrease offloading to adjust to the falling pressure.

Prefix Caching with Offloading

Prefix caching and parameter offloading are complementary mechanisms that both benefit from expanded KV cache capacity. Prefix caching avoids redundant prefill computation by retaining KV cache entries for shared prefixes, but its effectiveness depends on having sufficient memory to keep these entries resident. Parameter offloading frees GPU memory for KV cache, increasing capacity for both active requests and cached prefix entries. Additionally, vLLM’s KV cache offloading connector provides a secondary CPU memory tier for prefix cache entries, enabling evicted entries to be reloaded from CPU memory rather than recomputed. We evaluate how these mechanisms interact on a prefix-heavy workload.

Workload

We use the same synthetic document QA workload from Execution Optimizations in Part 2. The dataset consists of 16 documents of approximately 4,096 tokens each, with 200 questions per document drawn from a set of 10 question templates. Questions are shuffled across documents to simulate interleaved access patterns. Output lengths are sampled uniformly between 50 and 150 tokens. This creates 16 distinct prefix groups competing for cache space, representative of production workloads such as document understanding and retrieval-augmented generation.

Results

Similarly to what we described in Experimental Setup in Part 2, we serve requests via a Poisson process at fixed target arrival rates and report the achieved request rate of each system. Additionally, we modify the policy in Algorithm 1 to not decrease offloading when prefix caching is above a fixed user-defined threshold. Figure 14 shows median and P99 latency against achieved request rate for four configurations: standard vLLM, standard vLLM with KV cache offloading , dynamic offloading, and dynamic offloading with KV cache offloading.

Figure 14: Median (top) and P99 (bottom) E2E latency, TTFT, and TBT versus achieved request rate on the prefix-heavy workload for Qwen3-32B.

Standard vLLM saturates at approximately 2 RPS, at which point GPU KV cache capacity is exhausted by active requests and prefix cache entries are evicted, forcing subsequent requests sharing the same prefix to recompute the full 4,096-token prefill. Enabling KV cache offloading more than doubles this to approximately 5 RPS by preserving evicted prefix entries in CPU memory, though GPU KV cache capacity for active requests remains the bottleneck as arrival rates increase further.

Dynamic parameter offloading improves throughput over standard vLLM, with some runs achieving low latency at request rates up to 10 RPS. However, performance is highly unstable. This indicates that the offloading policy’s continuous adjustments to GPU memory allocation cause unpredictable eviction of prefix cache entries. Combining dynamic offloading with KV cache offloading reduces this variance but does not eliminate it. The CPU KV tier preserves some prefix entries that would otherwise be lost when the policy reclaims GPU capacity, resulting in more stable behavior than dynamic offloading alone. Substantial variability remains, however.

The variance at high request rates for the combined configuration reveals a limitation of the current design: the two mechanisms operate independently. The offloading policy adjusts GPU memory allocation based on KV cache utilization and the number of waiting requests, but is unaware which entries in the free KV cache block list contain important prefix data. Similarly, the KV cache offloading connector does not account for dynamic changes in GPU capacity. This lack of coordination can lead to suboptimal decisions. For example, the policy may reclaim KV cache capacity that holds high-value prefix entries without saving them to CPU, triggering unnecessary evictions and recomputations.

Conclusion

Discussion

We presented a dynamic parameter offloading system for LLM serving on the NVIDIA GH200 that exploits the NVLink-C2C interconnect to asynchronously prefetch offloaded model parameters while dynamically adjusting the offloading depth at runtime. By building on CUDA’s virtual memory management API, the system reallocates GPU memory between model parameters and KV cache without invalidating CUDA graphs, maintaining compatibility with production serving optimizations including prefix caching.

On the ShareGPT workload, we observe throughput improvements of 10% for Qwen3-32B, 16% for Llama 3.1-70B FP8, and 22% for Mixtral-8x22B over default vLLM. Both FP8 quantization and tensor parallelism shift the offloading tradeoff favorably: quantization halves per-layer transfer volume while retaining most of the compute window, and tensor parallelism extends the compute window through inter-GPU communication while reducing per-GPU transfer size. These effects widen the regime in which offloading overhead is outweighed by the capacity gain.

Beyond the limitations discussed in Limitations, our evaluation of Mixtral-8x22B revealed that the CUDA virtual memory 2 MB page alignment requirement limits the dynamic policy’s ability to react to fine-grained workload changes. Unlike Qwen3-32B and Llama 3.1-70B FP8, whose KV cache blocks are natively 2 MB-aligned, Mixtral-8x22B requires grouping multiple blocks into reclaimable units, coarsening the granularity at which memory can be redistributed.

On a synthetic prefix-cache-heavy workload, combining vLLM’s KV cache offloading with our dynamic parameter offloading yields up to a $2\times$ throughput improvement over standard vLLM, as the expanded GPU KV cache capacity admits more concurrent requests while keeping prefix entries in CPU memory. However, performance variability remains high because the two mechanisms operate independently: the offloading policy does not distinguish between free blocks and blocks holding valuable prefix data, and the KV cache offloading connector is unaware of dynamic GPU capacity changes.

At low request rates, the dynamic policy converges to minimal offloading, and our system performs comparably to default vLLM with negligible overhead. These results show that the policy can reduce unnecessary offloading under the tested low-load conditions. While high levels of offloading increase time between tokens due to longer decode iterations, the resulting capacity enables substantially higher concurrent request throughput. We therefore envision this system as particularly well-suited for absorbing traffic bursts and bridging sudden load increases while additional serving capacity is provisioned.

Future Work

The 2 MB page alignment used by our allocator is the primary obstacle to fine-grained dynamic memory redistribution. Future work could explore more aggressive block grouping strategies that co-locate KV cache blocks likely to be freed together, for instance by assigning grouped blocks to the same requests. Such data structures introduce scheduling overhead that must be carefully managed. vAttention explores driver modifications to support smaller allocation units; our implementation retains the 2 MB granularity. Additionally, adopting full CUDA graphs for the attention computation, while limiting graph splits to synchronization and transfer operations, could further reduce kernel launch overhead.

A natural extension of this work is a unified dynamic memory manager that jointly allocates HBM and CPU memory across model parameters, KV cache, and prefix cache entries based on workload characteristics. Such a system would coordinate offloading decisions with prefix cache eviction, avoiding the suboptimal independent operation observed in our evaluation. Reducing the virtual memory remapping cost for multi-GPU deployments, which currently scales super-linearly with GPU count, is essential for scaling dynamic offloading to larger tensor-parallel configurations. Additionally, multimodal workloads introduce additional memory tradeoffs through image preprocessing and encoder caches, whose retention must be balanced against KV cache capacity and parameters as the mix of text and image traffic varies.

More broadly, the principles underlying this system extend beyond single-model layer offloading. In multi-model pipelines — such as world models or end-to-end autonomous systems that chain perception, planning, and control models — each model could reside in CPU memory and be transferred to the GPU only when its stage in the pipeline is active. Since these models execute in a fixed sequential order, the same asynchronous prefetching strategy applies at the granularity of entire models rather than individual layers. This model-level offloading is particularly relevant for edge devices and robotics platforms in the physical AI domain, where GPU memory is scarce but the system must host multiple specialized models simultaneously.

entry.title: Profiling vLLM on the GH200
entry.content:
Introduction

In Part 1, we covered the background on LLM serving, the NVIDIA GH200 architecture, and the existing offloading landscape. In this post, we present an empirical analysis of vLLM’s performance on the GH200 Grace Hopper Superchip.

vLLM integrates the key optimizations described in Part 1 — continuous batching, chunked prefill, PagedAttention, and automatic prefix caching — into a unified, production-ready system. Its widespread adoption in both research and production environments, combined with its modular architecture and active development, makes it a representative target for studying LLM serving behavior on the GH200. Our analysis is based on vLLM v0.13.0, which uses the V1 engine architecture by default.

Our findings reveal several important implications: the GH200’s NVLink-C2C interconnect provides substantial bandwidth but vLLM’s current offloading mechanisms fail to exploit it, CUDA graphs are even more critical on the GH200 than on x86 systems, and a static offloading configuration is fundamentally limited. These observations motivate the design of our dynamic parameter offloading system, which we present in Part 3.

vLLM Architecture

vLLM has evolved substantially since its initial release, with features such as chunked prefill, prefix caching, and CUDA graphs transitioning from experimental to enabled by default. This section provides an overview of the current vLLM V1 architecture.

Overview

Figure 1: vLLM V1 engine architecture. Figure from .

The figure above illustrates the high-level architecture of vLLM’s V1 engine. Arriving requests are tokenized by the processor and forwarded to the engine core client, which communicates with the engine core via inter-process communication. This separation allows CPU-intensive tasks such as tokenization and detokenization to run concurrently with GPU-bound model execution. The engine core runs on the CPU and serves as the central coordinator, containing the scheduler, model executor, and KV cache manager. After inference completes, generated tokens are forwarded to the output processor for detokenization and streaming back to the client.

The engine core is the central component of vLLM and has a modular structure containing the scheduler, model executor, and KV cache manager. It runs a busy loop that repeatedly performs an engine step, where each step consists of invoking the scheduler to select which requests to advance, followed by dispatching the scheduled batch to the model executor for a forward pass.

Scheduler

vLLM handles two types of workloads: prefill and decode requests. The V1 scheduler can mix both types within a single batch but prioritizes decode requests, i.e., those already in the running queue. For each running request, the scheduler computes the number of new tokens to generate, allocates the required KV cache blocks, and updates the available token budget. If insufficient KV cache blocks are available, lower-priority requests are preempted and returned to the waiting queue, freeing their KV cache blocks for recomputation in a later step.

After processing decode requests, the scheduler handles prefill requests from the waiting queue. For each prefill request, the scheduler determines the required KV cache blocks. If prefix caching is enabled and requests share common prefixes, the corresponding blocks are shared rather than duplicated. Requests with sufficient KV cache capacity are promoted to the running queue and included in the batch dispatched to the model executor.

KV Cache Manager

Figure 2: KV Cache Management in vLLM. Figure from .

The KV cache manager handles KV cache block allocation and is central to enabling both PagedAttention and prefix caching. Importantly, the manager only maintains indexing structures, whereas the physical GPU memory is allocated and managed by the model workers.

The core data structure is a free list of available block IDs. Each block typically stores 16 tokens of KV cache data. When the scheduler requires blocks for a request, they are popped from this free list and associated with the request. When a request completes, its blocks are returned to the pool.

To support prefix caching, the manager additionally maintains a hash table mapping token sequences to their corresponding KV blocks. When a new request arrives, its token sequence is split into block-sized chunks and hashed. The scheduler looks up these hashes to identify blocks that have already been computed, either by active requests or by recently completed ones. Matching blocks are shared rather than recomputed, avoiding redundant prefill computation for common prefixes.

To track sharing, each block maintains a reference counter that increments when assigned to a request and decrements upon completion. Blocks are only returned to the free list when their reference count reaches zero, and cached blocks remain valid until they must be reallocated to accommodate new requests.

Model Executor

The model executor is responsible for running the forward pass of the model by coordinating workers, typically one per GPU. During initialization, each worker performs three key tasks: initializing its assigned device, loading the model weights, and allocating the KV cache. By default, vLLM allocates a separate KV cache tensor for each model layer, enabling compatibility with hybrid architectures that may have different KV cache requirements across layers (e.g., models combining attention and state-space layers).

CPU Offloading

KV Cache Offloading. vLLM supports asynchronous offloading and loading of KV cache data to CPU memory via the offloading connector API . This capability serves two primary use cases: (1) caching KV values for prefix sharing, where loading from CPU is faster than recomputation, and (2) preserving KV data for preempted requests, avoiding costly recomputation when requests are later rescheduled. vLLM recently introduced a new contiguous KV cache memory layout that stores all layers’ KV data in contiguous physical blocks, replacing the previous per-layer allocated layout. This change increased the effective block size from a few kilobytes to 0.5–2MB depending on the model and number of tokens in a block, improving direct memory access (DMA) transfer efficiency by an order of magnitude.

Weight Offloading. vLLM also supports offloading model parameters to CPU memory using unified virtual addressing (UVA), which allows the GPU to access CPU memory directly without explicit copies. While this approach enables serving models larger than GPU memory, it introduces a key limitation: data is fetched on-demand when accessed, preventing prefetching optimizations and resulting in higher latency for model weights not resident in GPU memory.

Neither KV cache offloading nor weight offloading is enabled by default in vLLM.

Experimental Setup

All experiments were conducted on the Alps supercomputer at the Swiss National Supercomputing Centre (CSCS).

Hardware. Each node contains four GH200 Grace Hopper Superchips. Each superchip pairs a 72-core ARM Neoverse V2 CPU with an H100 GPU, connected by a 900 GB/s cache-coherent NVLink-C2C interconnect. Memory per superchip comprises 96GB of HBM3 (4 TB/s bandwidth) on the GPU and 128GB (500 GB/s) of LPDDR5X on the CPU. The four superchips are fully connected via NVLink for GPU-to-GPU communication, and the node operates as a single NUMA system with 288 CPU cores and 4 GPUs.

Models and Workloads. We evaluate three model configurations: Qwen3-32B , a dense text-only transformer; Llama 3.1-70B with FP8 quantization, which fits on a single GH200 due to its reduced parameter size; and Mixtral-8x22B , a sparse mixture-of-experts model with 141B total parameters. Qwen3-32B and Llama 3.1-70B fit on a single GH200, while Mixtral-8x22B requires tensor parallelism across all four GPUs.

For text workloads, we use the ShareGPT dataset , which provides a representative distribution of real conversational prompt and completion lengths. For our end-to-end benchmarks, we generate an open-loop workload by sending requests to the vLLM engine according to a Poisson arrival process.

Metrics. We report the following latency metrics for each request:

  • Time to First Token (TTFT): Time from request arrival to generation of the first output token, reflecting responsiveness.
  • Time Between Tokens (TBT): Average time between successive output tokens during decoding.
  • End-to-End Latency (E2E Latency): Time from request arrival to completion.

Memory System Performance

The defining feature of the GH200 is its high-bandwidth NVLink-C2C interconnect between CPU and GPU. To characterize real-world transfer performance, we conducted microbenchmarks measuring achievable bandwidth in both directions.

Copy Performance

We implemented a PyTorch-based benchmark measuring transfer rates between CPU and GPU memory. Following best practices for maximizing DMA throughput, we used pinned (page-locked) CPU memory and asynchronous transfers via non-blocking copy operations. Bidirectional measurements used separate CUDA streams for each direction to enable concurrent transfers.

Figure 3: GH200 transfer bandwidth as a function of transfer size.

Directional asymmetry. As shown in the figure above, transfer performance exhibits significant asymmetry: CPU to GPU transfers achieve over 85% of peak theoretical bandwidth, whereas GPU to CPU transfers reach only approximately 35%. This disparity arises from the cache coherency protocol: transfers into CPU memory require additional coherency traffic to maintain consistency with the CPU cache hierarchy, overhead that is absent in the reverse direction. Similar behavior has been reported in prior work .

Size-dependent efficiency. Peak bandwidth is only attained for sufficiently large transfers: CPU to GPU requires tensors exceeding 128MB, while GPU to CPU saturates at 8MB. This difference reflects substantial fixed overhead that must be amortized, and suggests that small transfers will underutilize the interconnect.

Bidirectional contention. When transferring simultaneously in both directions, average per-direction bandwidth drops approximately 10% compared to the unidirectional GPU to CPU case, indicating contention for shared interconnect resources.

These findings suggest that applications should favor large, unidirectional transfers where possible to maximize effective bandwidth utilization. As we show in Part 3, our system is designed to exploit each of these characteristics: weight offloading leverages the higher CPU to GPU bandwidth, KV cache transfers are batched into large contiguous blocks to exceed saturation thresholds, and transfer scheduling avoids bidirectional contention wherever possible.

Managed vs. Pinned Memory

Related work demonstrated that transfers from HBM to managed memory allocated on the CPU achieve nearly twice the bandwidth of transfers from HBM to pinned CPU memory. While we were able to reproduce this result, we also observed significant performance degradation when performing repeated consecutive transfers. We hypothesize that this degradation stems from page table thrashing, potentially caused by the managed memory runtime’s page migration and coherency tracking mechanisms. This result is notable given that pinned memory is conventionally recommended for maximizing transfer bandwidth, suggesting that the GH200’s coherency architecture may favor managed memory allocations in certain access patterns.

This page migration overhead has also been identified as a critical bottleneck for LLM inference on the GH200 .

Execution Optimizations

vLLM provides several configurable optimizations that significantly affect serving performance. We evaluate CUDA graphs, prefix caching, and KV cache offloading to quantify their impact and identify limitations.

CUDA Graph Performance

Kernel launch overhead is particularly significant on the GH200, where the ARM-based Grace CPU exhibits lower single-threaded performance compared to x86 CPUs in traditional loosely-coupled systems . This makes CUDA graph capture especially important for minimizing CPU-side bottlenecks during decode iterations.

Figure 4: Impact of CUDA graphs on median and P99 TBT for Qwen3-32B on ShareGPT across request rates.

Enabling CUDA graphs reduces median decode time per token by over 40% at low request rates. While the absolute gap persists at higher load, the relative improvement narrows as GPU compute becomes the dominant bottleneck. Notably, piecewise CUDA graphs alone account for the majority of the observed benefit, with full graph capture providing only a marginal additional improvement. This is practical, as piecewise graphs offer greater flexibility in handling varying batch sizes without requiring capture of every possible shape.

Offloading Overhead

vLLM supports CPU offloading, enabling the use of CPU memory to store KV cache data and model parameters. Due to the overhead associated with transferring data between CPU and GPU, offloading is typically employed as a last resort for models or KV cache that exceed GPU memory capacity.

Notably, vLLM’s offloading implementations differ significantly between KV cache and parameter offloading. For KV cache offloading, vLLM employs asynchronous transfers with optimized memory layouts — reorganizing KV data into large, contiguous blocks to maximize DMA throughput . This creates a secondary caching tier in CPU DRAM from which previously computed KV data can be loaded back to the GPU faster than recomputation. However, this primarily benefits prefix-heavy workloads where requests share common prefixes. Crucially, KV cache offloading does not free GPU memory for additional concurrent requests, as active requests still require their KV data to reside on the GPU during decoding.

Figure 5: Impact of parameter and KV cache offloading on median E2E Latency, TTFT, TBT for Qwen3-32B on ShareGPT at 18.0 target arrival rate.

Parameter offloading relies on UVA, which allows the GPU to access CPU memory directly without explicit copies. While this simplifies implementation, data is fetched on-demand at the point of access rather than prefetched asynchronously. The freed GPU memory can then be used for KV cache, allowing for more requests to run concurrently. Each layer’s parameters are loaded only when needed, stalling execution while the transfer completes. This synchronous access pattern prevents the data movement overlap that the GH200’s NVLink-C2C interconnect could otherwise support.

The figure above confirms that neither strategy improves end-to-end latency under high load. KV offloading tracks the baseline closely, with only marginal wait time reductions from preemption recovery. UVA offloading frees enough GPU memory to eliminate queuing beyond approximately 23GB but the steadily increasing decode time per token from synchronous parameter fetching more than offsets this gain.

Prefix Caching Effectiveness

Agentic workloads, system prompts, and document understanding tasks often share common prefixes across requests. Prefix caching exploits this redundancy in two ways: it avoids redundant prefill computation, and it reduces memory usage by sharing KV cache blocks between requests.

Figure 6: Prefill time CDF with and without prefix caching.

To evaluate this, we construct a synthetic document QA workload where many requests share long common prefixes (≈ 4k tokens). The figure above shows the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of prefill times: with caching enabled, over 50% of requests achieve near-zero prefill latency due to cache hits, while cache misses show similar latency to the uncached baseline.

For deployments where the prefix cache exceeds GPU memory capacity, KV cache offloading to CPU DRAM could extend this benefit by providing a larger secondary cache tier, though at the cost of higher reload latency compared to GPU-resident cache hits.

Multimodal Inference

Multimodal serving introduces additional caching layers for image preprocessing and encoding, avoiding redundant computation when the same image appears across multiple requests. While benchmarking multimodal inference on the GH200, we identified a significant performance bottleneck: cache lookup required decoding the input image (e.g., JPEG to raw pixels) before computing its hash. For large 4K images, this decoding step alone can exceed 100ms, adding substantial latency even for cached images.

Figure 7: Comparison of image hashing strategies across image resolutions.

We addressed this by hashing the raw image bytes directly, bypassing the decoding step for cache hits. This reduces TTFT significantly for repeated images. Our fix was merged into vLLM , which bypasses image decoding for cache lookups and additionally reduces hash computation time by operating on the smaller compressed byte representation rather than decoded pixel data.

Implications for System Design

Our characterization reveals several key findings that motivate the design choices presented in Part 3.

The GH200’s NVLink-C2C interconnect provides substantial CPU to GPU bandwidth but vLLM’s current parameter offloading via UVA fails to exploit this. UVA fetches parameters synchronously at the point of access, preventing any overlap between data movement and computation. No prefetching is performed, and the interconnect’s full bandwidth is only realized for transfers exceeding 128MB, far larger than typical per-layer parameter accesses.

CUDA graphs are critical for decode performance on the GH200, reducing per-token latency by over 40%. Any offloading mechanism must therefore be compatible with CUDA graph capture to preserve this benefit rather than forcing fallback to eager execution.

Finally, while parameter offloading frees GPU memory for additional KV cache capacity, our results show that the decode penalty grows steadily with the amount offloaded, dominating any throughput gains from larger batch sizes. A static offloading configuration is therefore fundamentally limited: at low load, unnecessary offloading degrades decode performance without providing useful KV cache capacity, while at high load, insufficient offloading leaves throughput on the table. The optimal operating point depends on workload intensity, which varies at runtime.

These observations motivate the following design requirements:

Asymmetry-aware prefetching. Store offloaded parameters in contiguous CPU tensors and prefetch them asynchronously to the GPU, exploiting the favorable CPU to GPU bandwidth and enabling overlap with computation.

CUDA graph compatibility. Integrate parameter offloading with CUDA graph capture to maintain low kernel launch overhead during decode.

Dynamic adaptation. Adjust the offloading configuration at runtime based on KV cache pressure and iteration time, offloading parameters only when additional KV cache capacity is needed and sufficient compute exists to hide the data movement latency.

In Part 3, we present a system that addresses all three requirements.
